extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, practicing journalists, discourse analysts and linguistics researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative principles for how news stories (esp. AP-style) are organized and written — including ordering of facts, paragraphing, sentence length, use of connectives, quotes, and trade-offs between editor convenience and reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of Presentation of Facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The sequencing of sentences/facts in a story — e.g., chronological narrative order vs. the order used in the AP article. The text compares accounts by how many reorderings are required to make their sequences equivalent (Table 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure similarity of organization by minimal reorderings; note that fabricated narratives (Professor, Sheila, Reporter) are primarily chronological, while the AP account uses a non-chronological order (inverted-pyramid) and thus can be farthest from academic prose. Use ordering that matches the narrator's purpose: narratives for participants/observers -> chronological; news -> descending importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted Pyramid (lead and descending importance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard news structure: a summary lead followed by details arranged in descending order of importance (most important facts first, least important last).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize why it is used (editorial convenience, skimmability) and how it shapes content (emphasis on result over process). Criticisms include distortion, incoherence, temporal dislocation, loss of unities of time/place, and 'death' of story through exhaustion. Textbook definitions, lead/body/background/secondary breakdowns, and quotes from Brown, Mencher, and others illustrate the form and its rationales and failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block Paragraphing (paragraphs deletable independently)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice that each paragraph should stand as an independent unit that can be deleted without affecting the rest of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Block paragraphing eliminates transitions and anaphoric connections because paragraphs are written to be deletable; it increases reader inference demands and reinforces inverted-pyramid constraints. Anti-pattern: writing paragraphs so isolated that deleting one leaves no sense damage but reduces coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short Sentences (readability via sentence length)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines from Flesch/Gunning/AP/UP: keep sentences short (often cited target ~17 words) to increase readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices: split complex sentences at conjunctions, avoid or reduce semicolons, favor periods; textbooks urge short sentences as key to readable stories. Critique: shortening often removes explicit connectives and increases the inferencing burden on readers; short sentences may be 'choppy' and harm comprehension even while improving skimmability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short Paragraphs (visual/format reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Break longer paragraphs into smaller ones to produce white space, make pages look inviting, and allow easy deletions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although visually attractive and editor-friendly, short paragraphs can remove the final clue that adjacent sentences address the same point and thus make the story harder to integrate; the practice is driven by editorial convenience rather than logical organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Connectives and Transitions (explicit temporal/logical markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of explicit connectives (temporal: 'earlier', 'later'; logical: 'because', 'therefore'; causal: 'as a result') to make relations among facts explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AP account contains fewer connectives than other accounts. Textbooks advise transitions but often rely on superficial devices (repetition, pronouns, additive 'and') that do not guarantee coherence. Effective practice: use explicit logical/temporal connectives where they make the relation clear; beware relying solely on pronouns/repetition/sentence-pattern repetition to create coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Human-interest' details and quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of anecdotes, colorful details, and quotations (place them near the lead) to dramatize the story, provide 'pictures' and give verisimilitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: dramatize, attract readers, create impression of eyewitness credibility. Cautions: such details (e.g., color of a scarf) and quotations can be irrelevant, redundant, distract from the news point, and reduce clarity. When used only to 'brighten up' a story they may draw attention away from the main point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Irrelevant and Redundant Details
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude facts that are irrelevant to interpretation (e.g., the color of a protestor's scarf) and avoid redundant paraphrase/quotations that add no new information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a detail aids the reader's reasonable interpretation of significance; remove redundancies such as quoted signs that add nothing beyond the first sentence. Redundant or irrelevant material increases cognitive load and decreases clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of Organization with Communicative Goal / Narrator's Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of an account must reflect the narrator's goal (e.g., Professor: illustrate object of study, emphasize causes; Sheila: participant's stake and grievance; Reporter: satisfy audience curiosity and meet deadline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify narrator's motive and tailor what facts are highlighted and their order accordingly. The same event yields different organizations depending on narrator's purpose; more coherent accounts tend to be chronological, with variations determined by motive (e.g., advocacy vs neutral observation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance: Readability (attracting readers) vs Comprehensibility (logical organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic pedagogy emphasizes readability (short sentences, human interest, editor convenience) often at expense of logical organization and explicit connective use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation from the article: prioritize comprehensibility and logical organization over mere readability tricks. Teaching and editing should emphasize making the relevance of included information explicit, not just making copy 'flashy' or short. More connected writing can remain skimmable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead construction and priority ordering within story
rubrics_metrics.description: Deciding what fact(s) become the lead and the subsequent priority list: lead → material explaining/amplifying lead → necessary background → secondary material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks instruct reporters to make a priority list for the lead and body, but this often rests on the subjective criterion of 'decreasing importance.' Be explicit about why an item is prioritized: editorial convenience alone is insufficient justification for ordering that impairs comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution practices and restrictions on logical connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters are cautioned to attribute any statement that is not common knowledge or directly observed, which can limit the use of logical connectives that imply interpretation (e.g., 'therefore').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledging the reporter's ethic of objectivity, be aware that excessive literal attribution can prevent the writer from using useful logical connectives and so limit clarity. Balance attribution with clear signaling of inferential relations (use attribution where needed but do not let it eliminate necessary explicit connectives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical devices (repetition, pronouns, sentence-pattern repetition) are insufficient for coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbook advice to tie sentences together by repeating key words, using pronouns, synonyms, or repeating sentence patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices may give the appearance of connection but do not ensure logical coherence. The article gives counter-examples where such devices fail to create meaningful relations between propositions. Use them only as adjuncts to explicit connective and structural organization.
